caption:
Living with your partner 12 months? You're common-law. In Canada, after 12 months of living together, the CRA counts you as common-law, even if you never married.

WHY: the CRA treats someone as your common-law partner when you live together in a conjugal relationship for at least 12 continuous months (or sooner if you have a child together). After that, your benefits and credits are worked out from your family net income: your net income plus your partner's. That's the number the CRA uses for things like the Canada child benefit, so your benefits may drop.

HOW (10 minutes):
1. Sign in to CRA My Account.
2. Go to Profile, then Marital status, then Edit.
3. Pick common-law and the date your status changed.

THE CATCH: the CRA wants to hear by the end of the month after your status changed (moved in last October? the 12 months ended this October, so tell them by the end of November). If they later find they paid you too much, they send a notice and you pay it back. A short split of under 90 days doesn't restart the 12 months.

WHO THIS IS FOR: couples in Canada living together, not married, especially if either of you gets the Canada child benefit or the GST/HST credit.

Do this: update your marital status in CRA My Account.

Send this to the person you moved in with.

Part 2 is tomorrow (Mon) at 7 pm: why your partner has to file taxes every year, even with no income, to keep the Canada child benefit coming.

Education only, not financial advice.

Follow for one money rule a day, in plain words.

caption:
Partner didn't file a tax return? In Canada, to keep getting the Canada child benefit, you and your spouse or common-law partner each have to file a tax return every year, even with no income.

Part 2 of yesterday's post (living together 12 months makes you common-law for the CRA).

WHY: the Canada child benefit is worked out from your family net income: your net income plus your partner's. If one return is missing, the CRA can't work it out, and the CRA says payments will stop if you don't do your taxes. File late and payments may stop for a while.

HOW:
1. Each of you files your own return for 2026 by April 30, 2027.
2. Earned $0, or only tax-free income? Still file.
3. Check that your marital status is right in CRA My Account (Part 1).

THE CATCH: it's every year, not once. One missed return can pause the payments for the whole family.

WHO THIS IS FOR: parents in Canada who get the Canada child benefit, especially when one partner stays home, studies or earns nothing.

Do this: both of you: file by April 30, 2027.

Send this to the partner who "didn't need to file".

There's no joint return in Canada: two returns, every year.

Education only, not tax advice.

Follow for one money rule a day, in plain words.

caption:
Too sick to make decisions? Who pays your bills? In Ontario, if illness or an accident leaves you unable to make decisions and you have no continuing power of attorney for property, your family, including your spouse, can't automatically manage your money.

WHY: a continuing power of attorney for property is a document where you name the person who can handle your bank accounts, bills and home, and 'continuing' means it can still be used after you're no longer able to make those decisions yourself. Without one, Ontario says your family might have to go to court to become your court-appointed guardian, and the government may have to make decisions through the Office of the Public Guardian and Trustee, as a last resort.

HOW (one evening):
1. Search 'Ontario power of attorney kit' and download the free kit (Ministry of the Attorney General).
2. Fill in the Continuing Power of Attorney for Property. Name someone you trust: your spouse, a family member or a long-time friend. They don't have to be a lawyer.
3. Sign it in front of two witnesses. Your attorney and their spouse or partner can't be witnesses, and nor can anyone under 18 (the kit lists who else can't).
4. Tell your person where it is.

THE CATCH: it only works if you sign it while you can still decide. If your money is complicated, Ontario suggests a lawyer. This is Ontario's rule; other provinces have their own.

WHO THIS IS FOR: adults in Ontario, married or not, with a bank account, bills or a home someone may need to manage.

Do this: sign a continuing power of attorney for property.

Send this to your partner, so you both do it.

Education only, not legal or financial advice.

Follow for one money rule a day, in plain words.

caption:
Money talk only in a fight? The habit: book a 20-minute money date, same day every month, alone or with your partner.

Rich Habits, Decoded No. 5. Each episode takes one money habit and shows you how to do it on a normal paycheque.

WHY IT WORKS: when money only comes up after a surprise bill, every talk starts stressed. A short, booked check-in turns it into a routine: you see the month before it surprises you, and you only decide one thing at a time.

HOW (20 minutes, once a month):
1. Pick a fixed day, like the 7th, and put it in both calendars.
2. Open your bank and card apps side by side.
3. Ask three questions: What came in this month? What went out? What's the next big bill?
4. Pick one thing to change next month, then stop when the timer ends.

THE CATCH: keep it short and kind. It's a check-in, not a trial. If one of you carries debt the other didn't know about, start with that.

Do this: put a 20-minute money date in your calendar, same day every month.

Send this to the person you share bills with.

Rich Habits, Decoded No. 6 is Friday at 5 pm.

Education only, not financial advice.

Follow for one money rule a day, in plain words.
